name: Full-stack developer
summary: Full-stack developer interviews usually check that you can build a feature end to end: a working interface, the API behind it and the database underneath. Candidates commonly report a take-home or live exercise building a small app, then questions on JavaScript or the role's main language, databases and deployment; experienced candidates are often asked to design a whole feature.
rounds: Take-home or online test: often a small app with a frontend, an API and a database
Technical interview: walk through your code, then extend or fix it live
Fundamentals across the stack: JavaScript, a framework, APIs, databases and deployment
Feature or system design for experienced roles
looks_for: Building something that works end to end, not just one layer
Knowing where logic belongs: browser, server or database
Sound data modelling and API design
Security basics on both sides: validation, authentication and secrets
Getting code deployed and running, not only working locally
Pragmatism: choosing simple tools and shipping

questions.text: Tell me about a time you delivered a feature on your own across frontend and backend under a deadline.
covers: The scope, and what you cut to make the deadline
How you split the work between screens, API and data
What shipped and what you cleaned up afterwards

questions.text: Describe a bug that turned out to be in a different layer from where you first looked.
covers: The symptom and where you first looked
How you traced it across the browser, network, server and database
The real cause and what it taught you about debugging

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to learn a new framework or tool quickly for a project.
covers: Why it was needed and how much time you had
How you learned: the docs, a small prototype, someone experienced
What you built, and what you'd do differently

questions.text: Tell me about a time you pushed back on a feature request or suggested a simpler way to do it.
covers: The request and the cost you saw in it
The simpler option and how you made the case
The outcome for users and the team

questions.text: Walk me through an app you've built: the stack, how data flows from a click to the database, and why you chose each part.
covers: A short picture of the frontend, API, database and hosting
One request traced from the click to the database and back
A choice you'd make differently now, and why

questions.text: Talk me through how you'd build a simple notes app with login, from the database tables up to the screens.
covers: Tables or collections for users and notes, with each note tied to its owner
API endpoints that check the user is logged in and owns the note on every request
Screens with loading and error states, and how it gets deployed

questions.text: Where should input validation happen: in the browser, on the server, or both? Why?
covers: The browser for quick feedback to users
The server because anything sent from a client can be changed
Database constraints as a last line of defence

questions.text: How does a login session work across the frontend and backend? Compare cookies and tokens.
covers: Server-side sessions with a cookie versus self-contained signed tokens
Where tokens are stored and the risks of each: cross-site scripting, CSRF
Expiry, logout and refreshing a session

questions.text: What is CORS, and why might a request work from Postman or curl but fail from the browser?
covers: The browser's same-origin rule, and what CORS headers allow
Preflight requests for some methods and headers
Fixing it on the server by allowing the right origins, not a wildcard everywhere

questions.text: In a MERN-style app, when would you use MongoDB, and when would a relational database be the better choice?
covers: Documents suit nested data that's read together; relational suits many relationships and joins
Consistency needs, such as orders and payments
Explaining the choice you made in your own project

questions.text: How do you deploy a full-stack app, and how do you keep secrets such as API keys out of the code?
covers: A build step, hosting for the frontend and the API, and a managed database
Environment variables or a secrets manager, never committed to Git
Separate settings for development, staging and production

questions.text: A list page gets slow once there are thousands of records. What would you change across the stack?
covers: Pagination or infinite scroll instead of loading everything
An index for the query, and returning only the fields the page needs
Caching, and a loading state so the page feels responsive

questions.text: How would you add live updates, such as chat messages or order status, to an existing web app?
covers: Polling, server-sent events and WebSockets, and when each fits
Reconnecting, and messages that arrive late or out of order
Making it work with more than one server

questions.text: When an API changes, how do you keep the frontend and backend in step?
covers: Shared types or an API schema, and versioning
Tests that check the API contract
Changing in steps so older clients keep working

questions.text: Talk me through how you'd let users upload and display a profile photo safely.
covers: Checking file type and size on the server, not just in the browser
Storing files in object storage rather than the database, and serving them through a CDN
Resizing images, and controlling who can see them

questions.text: Do you see yourself leaning more towards frontend or backend over time? Why?
covers: An honest answer, with an example of work you enjoyed
Why knowing the whole stack still helps in that direction
What you're learning now

questions.text: Why do you want to work here as a full-stack developer?
covers: Something specific about the product or its users
How your experience fits the stack the team uses
What you'd hope to own in your first year

tips: Treat a take-home like work you'd ship: a README, clear setup steps, a few tests and a note on what you'd do with more time.
Expect to change your take-home live; know your own code well enough to extend it without searching.
Have a deployed project with a live link; it shows you can get past 'works on my machine'.
Say which layer you're talking about as you answer; full-stack answers get muddled quickly otherwise.
Don't list every technology you've touched; pick the stack you know best and be ready to go deep on it.
